fact: USA has solid yellow center lines and white edge lines on the right. Road lines are always yellow on the left edge, white on the right edge of the road.
UK bollards are round with reflective bands — white at the top, red below. Ireland bollards are similar but have yellow reflective bands instead of red.
French bollards are square/concrete with a flat top, white body, and a single orange reflective stripe near the top — unmistakable once you know it.
Finland has distinctive two-arm power poles ('Finnish Y-poles') where the crossbars form a subtle V or Y shape. Ground-mounted transformers on concrete bases are also common.
Swedish utility poles often have three crossbars in a stepped configuration. Look for the distinctive trunk-mounted fuse boxes and insulators on angled brackets.

In the southern hemisphere, the sun is in the northern part of the sky. Since Google car covers face north/south, Australia & NZ coverage shows the sun to the north — opposite of what you'd expect in Europe/USA.

German-speaking countries use white-on-blue highway signs (Autobahn) with serif fonts. Town signs are yellow with black text. Look for Ausfahrt (exit), Straße (street), and the distinctive Bundesstraße yellow signs with black numbers.

Italian road signs feature green backgrounds for motorways and blue for local roads. Town name signs have a distinctive red border with two towers icon. Architecture is a huge clue — terracotta roofs, shuttered windows, narrow medieval streets.

Japanese license plates are white with green text (standard) or yellow with green text (kei cars). The plate format shows the city/region name in kanji at the top. Signs use blue/white with both Japanese characters and Romanized text.

South Africa has red/white bollard reflectors (like the UK) but drives on the left. The landscape is distinctive — flat-topped table mountains, dry savanna, and aloe plants. License plates are white/yellow (front/rear) with provincial codes like GP (Gauteng), WC (Western Cape).
